scenario: AITA for not hosting thanksgiving like I planned to | For about 50 years, my mom hosted all of her children and grandchildren for thanksgiving and Christmas Eve. She’s now gotten too old and asked us kids to take over the tradition. There are 4 of us so we just rotate. We’ve each hosted one holiday so far. This thanksgiving is my turn. We have never spent thanksgiving or Christmas Eve with my wife’s family. We’ve just never been as close to them plus they live all over the country. Well this year her mom and aunts decided to go to the Macy’s thanksgiving day parade. At first it was just a sister’s trip but then they decided to invite all their kids and grandkids to meet them up there. My wife really wants to go. She hasnt seen some of her aunts and cousins in years. Our daughter wants to go because it’s a “once in a lifetime event” (which i agree with). And I want to go. As soon as we decided to go I called my older brother to see what we should do about thanksgiving because I can’t host this year. He said our oldest sister is going to be pissed and i have to tell her myself. He wished me luck. So I call her and she is mad. She says she’ll probably have to end up hosting even though she is up next for Christmas and I’m being inconsiderate of what our mom asked us to do. “Mom wouldn’t abandon thanksgiving to go to nyc” and went on about how sad mom will be that I’m doing this. I offered to pay for them to rent a spot and have it catered but she said that takes away from the close knit family vibe. My brother said his wife might be up for it but he didn’t sound too happy about asking her. My other sister can’t do it because she’s renovating her house. I do feel bad for backing out of my turn but I tried to offer up solutions and I also offered to host the next holiday—which my oldest sister said no to because it’s her turn and she’s been planning for it all year. Next up is my brother so I said me and him could maybe just swap thanksgivings if his wife is up for it. Am I in the wrong here?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I'm in the wrong here. Let me start by understanding the situation. My mom has been hosting Thanksgiving and Christmas Eve for about 50 years, and now she's too old, so we, her four kids, are supposed to take over the tradition by rotating. Each of us has hosted one holiday so far, and this Thanksgiving is my turn. But here's the thing: my wife's family decided to go to the Macy's Thanksgiving Day parade this year, and they invited all their kids and grandkids. My wife really wants to go because she hasn't seen some of her aunts and cousins in years, and our daughter is excited too because it's a once-in-a-lifetime event. I also want to go. So, as soon as we decided to go, I called my older brother to figure out what to do about Thanksgiving since I can't host this year. He said our oldest sister is going to be mad and that I have to tell her myself. He wished me luck. When I called her, she was mad. She said she'll probably have to end up hosting even though it's her turn for Christmas, and I'm being inconsiderate of what our mom asked us to do. She also mentioned that Mom wouldn't abandon Thanksgiving to go to New York and went on about how sad Mom will be that I'm doing this. I offered to pay for them to rent a place and have it catered, but she said that takes away from the close-knit family vibe. My brother mentioned his wife might be up for it, but he didn't sound too happy about asking her. My other sister can't do it because she's renovating her house. I feel bad for backing out of my turn, but I tried to offer solutions and even offered to host the next holiday, which my oldest sister said no to because it's her turn and she's been planning for it all year. Next up is my brother, so I suggested that maybe me and him could swap Thanksgivings if his wife is up for it. Am I in the wrong here? I'm not sure. On one hand, I want to spend Thanksgiving with my wife's family, and it seems like a special opportunity. On the other hand, I agreed to take over the tradition, and now I'm backing out, which is making my sister upset and potentially disrupting the family plans. I guess I need to think about the importance of family traditions and the commitments we made to our mom. It's been a long-standing tradition, and my mom worked hard to keep it going for 50 years. By rotating, we're supposed to honor that tradition. But at the same time, my wife's family is important to me, and this parade seems like a unique experience. I also feel like I'm trying to make it work by offering solutions, like paying for a place or swapping with my brother. Maybe I'm not entirely in the wrong, but I could have handled it better. Perhaps I should have communicated earlier with my sister and the rest of the family about my intentions to go to the parade. If I had talked it through beforehand, maybe we could have found a compromise or adjusted the plans accordingly. Also, by offering to pay for a place, I'm trying to mitigate the impact of my absence, but my sister feels that it's taking away from the family vibe. That makes me realize that money isn't the only factor here; it's about the emotional connection and the shared experience. In the end, I think I need to weigh the importance of family traditions against the personal opportunity with my wife's family. If the tradition is something we all value deeply, then maybe I should prioritize that. But if the opportunity with my wife's family is truly once-in-a-lifetime, then it might be worth rethinking the tradition for this year. I also need to consider how my actions affect my siblings and the overall family dynamics. My sister is clearly upset, and that's a valid concern. Maybe I should have been more considerate of her feelings and the effort she's putting into hosting. Perhaps the best approach is to have an open and honest conversation with my sister and the rest of the family to understand everyone's perspectives and find a solution that works for everyone. That way, we can either adjust the plans or find a way to make both opportunities work, if possible. In summary, while I'm not entirely in the wrong, there could have been better ways to handle the situation by communicating earlier and considering the emotional and traditional aspects of the family gatherings.
